Tally, in detail, because it is the one that matters

Tally is the statutory book of record in most Indian firms and will stay that way. So this is deliberately an integration and not a replacement, and the value is not speed — it is that nobody types the same voucher twice.

The load-bearing feature is that each voucher's remote ID is deterministic, so re-exporting a batch updates the voucher already in Tally instead of creating a second one. Ledgers and cost centres have to be mapped first, which is why the screen leads with the count of mappings that are broken or switched off. An inactive mapping does not fail loudly — the transactions are simply absent from the batch, and the two systems disagree weeks later.

One constraint to know before you plan around it. Tally is a Windows application in the accounts room, answering on a loopback or a 192.168 address, and a cloud server cannot reach that. A direct push has to be switched on per connection by an administrator against one exact stored host, and link-local addresses stay refused whatever the flag says, because that is where the cloud metadata service lives. The common path is simpler: download the file and import it from Tally's Gateway, Import Data. The screen tells you which of the two your setup allows, in a sentence, rather than a green dot that means nothing.

GSTR-2B, in detail

Input tax credit is claimable only to the extent it appears in GSTR-2B, which the government builds from what your suppliers filed. An invoice in your books your supplier never uploaded is not credit — it is a receivable from a supplier who has your money. So the figure the screen leads with is credit at risk.

  • It is a file import, not a portal connection. Both formats are accepted, the portal JSON and the Excel or CSV export. We never log into GSTN for you.
  • The raw file is stored before it is parsed, and a parse failure never rolls that away. The file is the evidence, and a parse bug is found a year later at a notice.
  • A partial parse is a failure, not a success. A row skipped quietly looks exactly like a supplier who did not file, so you chase an innocent supplier while the Section 16(4) clock runs on a credit you were entitled to.
  • The two directions are reported separately, never netted into one unmatched count. In books but not in 2B is money at risk today. In 2B but not in books is a missing bill, or somebody billing you for what you never bought.
  • Filing a period is a one-way door, and a reconciliation whose own arithmetic does not balance cannot be filed at all.

What is not built, said plainly

One of these is on the roadmap. The rest are honest noes.

  • E-invoicing. No IRP connection, no IRN, no signed QR. If your turnover puts you inside the threshold you will keep generating IRNs the way you do today. This is the gap we hear about most and the one most likely to close first.
  • E-way bill. Number and date are captured on the challan so it prints correctly. Generation happens on the NIC portal, by a person.
  • WhatsApp Business API. Notices render as plain text in six languages, sized for a message, and every lead carries a channel — but you paste it yourself. A real connection means a business account, template approval and per-message cost, and we would rather build it properly for a customer who needs it than half-build it for a logo.
  • Payment gateways for collecting from customers. A bounced cheque correctly releases the allocation and recomputes interest from the original due date, but the callback that would automate receipt entry does not exist. We use a gateway for our own subscription billing; that is our plumbing, not yours.
  • Banks. No feed, no statement import, no reconciliation screen. This is the one on the list we are least comfortable about.

What we will never build

A Tally replacement. Not because it would be hard, but because the auditor asks for Tally by name, and being the second-best answer to a question nobody is asking is a poor use of a small team.

Scraping the GST portal with your credentials. Some products do this. It means handing your login to a third party and depending on a page layout the government changes without notice. We import a file you downloaded, and that is the line.

Custom integrations

Anything specific to your business is scoped and quoted separately, named on your scope sheet before you sign. For many cases you will not need us: automations include an outbound HTTP step, so a workspace can push a record to a service you already pay for with no code from us.

  • An automation runs with the permissions of a named person, never as the engine. It can do nothing its author could not do by hand.
  • Outbound requests are blocked from loopback, private ranges and link-local. That closes server-side request forgery, and it also means an automation cannot reach a device on your own office network. Tally is the one exception, and it is opt-in, audited and host-locked.
  • Bespoke work is priced once we have seen the other side's documentation. If their API is bad we will say so before you commit, not after.

Questions people actually ask

Our CA wants everything in Tally. Does this fight with that?

No, it is designed around it. Operations run in Ordence, vouchers export into Tally, and the export is re-runnable without duplicating.

Will you build the e-invoice integration for us?

Possibly, and it would be quoted. It is the most requested missing piece, so if your turnover requires it, raise it in the first conversation rather than the fourth. It changes the shape of the scope.

Tell us the one thing that has to connect.

Usually there is exactly one, and usually it is Tally. Name it and we will tell you whether it is built, buildable, or a no.
